title: NCLAT: Director Can't Set Off Dues to Sister Firms He Never Proved Were Related to Dodge IBC Threshold
seo_title: NCLAT Rejects Set-Off Bid to Dodge IBC Threshold
meta_description: NCLAT New Delhi upholds Tycoons Industries' insolvency admission, rejecting a director's bid to set off unrelated dues below the IBC threshold.
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
case_name: Joy Deb Chatterjee v. Kokila Mining and Neehal Mahamulal Pathan
body: A former director's attempt to shrink a mining-equipment debt below the threshold needed to trigger insolvency proceedings has failed before the NCLAT's New Delhi bench, which upheld the admission of Tycoons Industries Private Limited into corporate insolvency resolution. Kokila Mining had supplied heavy mining equipment on lease to Tycoons for coal mining sites in Jharkhand under work orders executed in August 2022 and July 2023, and brought a Section 9 petition before the NCLT's Chandigarh bench when the dues went unpaid.

Kokila Mining's case was that more than Rs 10.72 crore remained outstanding after adjusting a Rs 30 lakh payment it had received from a Tycoons vendor against the total. The NCLT Chandigarh bench admitted the petition on 11 June 2026, rejecting the set-off defence Tycoons had raised, and Joy Deb Chatterjee, a former director of the company, carried the fight to the appellate tribunal.

Chatterjee's central argument on appeal was that dues owed by certain entities he described as sister concerns of Kokila Mining ought to be set off against the operational debt claimed, and that doing so would pull the outstanding amount below the statutory threshold for admitting a Section 9 petition. He also raised a pre-existing dispute defence and separately challenged the validity of the demand notice, arguing it had been served at Tycoons' corporate office rather than its registered office.

The Appellate Tribunal was unmoved on each point. On the set-off claim, it found that Chatterjee had produced no evidence establishing that the entities whose liabilities he wanted adjusted against Kokila Mining's claim were in fact sister concerns of the operational creditor at all, so there was nothing on record to set off against anything. On the pre-existing dispute, the Tribunal pointed to a reconciliation statement that acknowledged the dues, along with the debt's appearance in the records of an Information Utility as deemed authenticated, and held that Tycoons had failed to substantiate any genuine dispute predating the demand notice.

On the service question, the Tribunal treated delivery of the demand notice at either the corporate office or the registered office of the corporate debtor as valid service for the purposes of Section 8 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, declining to read the provision as demanding delivery at the registered address specifically to the exclusion of any other office at which the company could be reached. Chatterjee's argument had been that a notice sent anywhere other than the registered office could not trigger the ten-day clock within which a corporate debtor must either pay the operational debt or point to a pre-existing dispute, and that a defective notice should have been fatal to the whole petition at the admission stage itself. The Tribunal did not accept that a company actually carrying on business from, and apparently receiving correspondence at, its corporate office could complain of prejudice merely because the notice went there rather than to the address on its incorporation papers.

With all three defences rejected, the Tribunal dismissed Chatterjee's appeal and left the CIRP admission against Tycoons Industries undisturbed, meaning the resolution process Kokila Mining set in motion through the Chandigarh bench continues as before. The former director's attempt to reopen the threshold question at the appellate stage, after having already lost it before the NCLT, did not get any further traction. Once a resolution professional takes charge under an admitted CIRP, the kind of arguments Chatterjee raised, about the true size of the debt or the propriety of the notice that preceded the petition, generally have to be made at the earliest possible stage; running them again on appeal after the tribunal of first instance has already rejected them on the facts is an uphill climb, and this order shows why.

For operational creditors chasing dues from a corporate debtor that tries to manufacture a set-off out of a third party's unrelated liabilities, the ruling is a reminder that the burden sits squarely on the debtor to prove the relationship it is relying on, not merely to assert it. A bare claim that another entity is a sister concern of the creditor, without documents showing common ownership, control or some other connection, will not do the work of pulling a claim below the insolvency threshold. Corporate debtors would do better to raise and document any genuine set-off or dispute before a demand notice arrives, rather than constructing one afterward in the hope that an unsubstantiated assertion survives scrutiny at either the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal.
why_it_matters: The ruling confirms that a corporate debtor resisting a Section 9 petition cannot lower the claimed debt below the insolvency threshold by asserting a set-off against entities it has not shown are actually related to the operational creditor; the relationship itself must be proved, not merely alleged. It also affirms that service of a demand notice at a corporate debtor's corporate office, as distinct from its registered office, can satisfy Section 8 of the Code, giving operational creditors more practical room in how they serve notice before filing.
card_summary: NCLAT New Delhi upholds CIRP admission against Tycoons Industries, rejecting a former director's bid to set off unrelated third-party dues and dodge the IBC's debt threshold.
card_tip: Claiming a set-off against an operational creditor's 'sister concern' will not reduce a debt below the IBC threshold unless you can prove the two entities are actually related.
verification_notes: Case name, citation (Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1125 of 2026), decision date (17 November 2026), background facts (the NCLT Chandigarh admission of 11 June 2026, the Rs 10.72 crore figure, the work orders and the Jharkhand mining sites), and the Tribunal's reasoning on set-off, pre-existing dispute, and service of the demand notice are taken from two LiveLaw Biz reports, one covering the NCLAT appeal and one covering the earlier NCLT Chandigarh admission. I did not locate a report from a second, independent outlet on either stage of this matter; coverage appears limited to LiveLaw Biz. The exact coram (names of the Members on the NCLAT bench) was not confirmed in the sources reviewed and is therefore not stated. NCLAT New Delhi is the Delhi-based appellate forum in this matter, though the underlying parties and the NCLT bench of first instance are in Chandigarh and Jharkhand respectively.
